_comment: Example narration for the bundled example scenes, explaining a fictional Acme checkout design doc. One scene per concept; one beat per spoken sentence and visual cue. A beat is a string or {say, show, hold}: say is spelled for the ear, show is the caption in real spelling (defaults to say with spelled letters rejoined), hold is extra silence in seconds. title names the chapter, source is the on-screen source tag, visuals lists every box, arrow, and count the scene draws so the fact pass can check pictures as well as words. Replace this with the real lecture.

scenes.title: Two taps, one order?

boxes: topic pills: request path, the change, failures, open questions

beats: A customer taps Pay, the page hangs, and they tap it again.
This walkthrough follows one order through the Acme checkout design to answer that.
We'll trace the request, look at the change that makes retries safe, break a few dependencies, and finish with what's still open.

scenes.title: The path of a request

arrows: Client -> API gateway -> Order service -> Database: request
Database -> Order service -> API gateway -> Client: confirmation

beats: Let's start with the path a request takes.
It enters at the A P I gateway, which checks who you are and how fast you're calling.
Next, the order service validates the cart and reserves the stock.
Then the database records the order, exactly once.

beats.say: Now watch one request travel all the way down, and the confirmation come back up.

scenes.title: The change that makes retries safe

boxes: orders table with one row per tap
illustrative: two taps (the scenario from the intro, not a measured count)

beats: Here's the part of the design that answers our question.
Before, every retry inserted a brand new order.
Now each request carries an idempotency key, created once by the client.

beats.say: If that key was already used, the service returns the original order instead of writing a second one.

beats: So two taps make one order, and one charge.

scenes.title: Failures stay contained

illustrative: packet dots show traffic, not a rate

beats: What happens when a dependency breaks?
If the cache goes down, reads get slower, but every order still goes through.
If a database replica fails, the primary keeps taking writes.

beats.say: And if the payment provider times out, the charge waits in a queue and retries, instead of failing the order.

scenes.title: Agreeing across services
beats: Placing an order touches three services, so they have to agree.
First, the coordinator asks every service to prepare.
Each one holds what it needs, but doesn't commit anything yet.
Once all three say they're ready, the coordinator tells them to commit, all together.
And if any one of them says no, everyone aborts, so nothing is ever half done.

scenes.title: The life of an order
beats: Every order moves through a small set of states.
It starts as pending, and becomes paid once the charge clears.
From paid, it ships, and finally it's delivered.
At any point before shipping, it can be cancelled instead.
Delivered and cancelled are final. Once an order lands in one, it never moves again.

scenes.title: Where this is headed
beats: So where is this headed?

beats.say: In the first quarter of twenty twenty-seven, payments moves into its own service.
beats.show: In Q1 2027, payments moves into its own service.

beats: In the second, checkout runs in a second region.
In the third, customers can edit an order after placing it.
And by the end of the year, the old monolith is retired.

scenes.title: What to check

boxes: not verified: taps in two regions
open: how long keys are kept

beats: Before you sign off, here's what the design settles, and what it leaves open.
One decision: the client creates the idempotency key, not the server.
The double tap has a test. Two requests with one key make exactly one order.
What isn't covered yet is two taps landing in different regions.
And the doc doesn't say how long a key is remembered. That's an open question.

beats.say: Those last two are where your review time is best spent.

scenes.title: Recap

boxes: takeaways: one key per order, failures degrade, two open questions
end card: source, revision, date, voice

beats: So, two taps, one order.
Every request carries a key, failures slow things down instead of failing the order, and two questions are still open.

beats.say: Everything in this video comes from the Acme checkout design doc, revision four.

beats: Thanks for watching.
